books.title: Predictably Irrational
books.author: Dan Ariely
books.why: Shows that our slips with prices, effort and choice follow patterns we can learn to spot in ourselves.

cards.title: We judge by comparison
cards.body: We rarely know what something is worth on its own, so we compare it with whatever sits beside it. Sellers use this by adding an option nobody is meant to pick, such as a slightly worse deal at the same price, which makes its neighbour look like a bargain. A middling bottle of wine sells better once a very expensive one appears on the list above it.
cards.try: The next time you see three options side by side, ask which one is only there to make another look good.

cards.title: The first number sticks
cards.body: The first price we meet for something becomes the yardstick for every later price, even when that first number was arbitrary. The book describes experiments in which an unrelated number people had just written down shifted what they offered to pay for goods. This is why the crossed-out "original" price on a tag does its work even when you doubt it was ever charged.

cards.title: Free is not just a low price
cards.body: When something costs nothing we stop weighing costs against benefits and simply grab it. Ariely argues that zero removes the fear of losing out, so a free item feels far better than a very cheap one of greater value. You see it when you add a book you do not want to an order to reach free delivery, and end up spending more than the delivery would have cost.

cards.title: Two rule books: social and market
cards.body: We live by social rules (favours, warmth, no bill) and market rules (prices, wages, contracts). Trouble starts when they mix. Offering to pay a friend for helping you move turns a kindness into a badly paid job, and both of you feel worse. A small gift or a shared meal keeps the exchange social. Once money enters, the social rules are slow to return.

cards.title: Owning something inflates its worth
cards.body: Once a thing is ours we value it more than we did before, and more than any buyer will. We focus on what we would lose by parting with it, while the buyer only sees the price. This is why people overprice their own house or car, and why free trial periods work: after a month the product feels like yours, and giving it back feels like a loss.
cards.try: Pick one thing you are holding on to and ask: if I did not own this, what would I pay to get it today?

cards.title: How far to trust the experiments
cards.body: The broad effects in this book, such as anchoring, decoy options and overvaluing what we own, have been found by many researchers. But some individual experiments it describes have not held up when repeated, and some of Ariely's later research on honesty has been seriously questioned. Read it as a map of tendencies worth watching for, and do not lean on any single study or exact figure.

books.title: Stumbling on Happiness
books.author: Daniel Gilbert
books.why: Explains why we are so often wrong about what will make us happy, and what to do instead.

cards.title: Imagination is a sketchy forecaster
cards.body: We decide what to pursue by imagining how it will feel, and Gilbert's argument is that this picture is unreliable. Imagination quietly fills in details that will not be there and leaves out ones that will. Picture a holiday and you see the beach, not the queues, the heat or the argument about dinner. The forecast feels like a preview, but it is closer to a rough sketch.

cards.title: We overestimate how long feelings last
cards.body: People expect good and bad events to affect them more strongly and for longer than they do. The promotion will not keep you elated for a year, and the failed exam will not flatten you for a year either. Life fills up again with ordinary things that take your attention. Knowing this makes big decisions lighter: most outcomes will matter less to your mood than you fear or hope.

cards.title: The mind's quiet repair system
cards.body: Gilbert describes a kind of psychological immune system. After a real setback we find new ways to see it: the job was not right anyway, the break-up taught us something. We do this without noticing, so we do not count on it in advance, and that is one reason we overrate how bad things will feel. It switches on more reliably for serious blows than for small daily irritations.

cards.title: We grow to like what we cannot undo
cards.body: We want the freedom to change our minds, yet the book argues we end up more content with choices that are final. When a decision can be reversed we keep checking whether it was right. When it cannot, the mind gets to work finding what is good about it. A purchase with a thirty-day return window can leave you less satisfied than one you simply have to live with.

cards.title: Today's mood colours tomorrow
cards.body: We imagine the future through whatever we feel now. Shop for food when hungry and you buy too much; plan next week when exhausted and everything looks impossible. The present leaks into the forecast and we do not correct for it enough. It helps to notice your current state before deciding anything about a future in which you will feel different.
cards.try: Before you make a plan today, name your mood first and ask if you would decide the same way after a meal and a rest.

cards.title: Ask someone who is already there
cards.body: Gilbert's most practical advice is to stop imagining and ask. The feelings of a person who is living the experience now are a better guide than your own picture of it. Thinking about moving to a small town or changing careers? Ask someone doing it how their ordinary Tuesday feels. We resist this because we believe we are unlike other people, but in our emotional reactions we are more alike than we suppose.
cards.try: Thinking over a decision? Find one person already living that choice and ask what a normal day is like.

books.title: The Happiness Hypothesis
books.author: Jonathan Haidt
books.why: Tests ten old ideas about the good life against modern psychology and keeps what holds up.

cards.title: The rider and the elephant
cards.body: Haidt pictures the mind as a small rider on a large elephant. The rider is conscious reasoning; the elephant is everything else: gut feelings, habits, cravings, fears. The rider can advise and steer a little, but cannot drag the elephant where it does not want to go. This is why knowing you should stop scrolling does not stop you. Lasting change means training the elephant, not lecturing it.

cards.title: The mind leans toward the bad
cards.body: We react more quickly and strongly to threats and setbacks than to good things of the same size. One critical remark outweighs several kind ones. This once kept our ancestors alive, but it tilts the elephant toward worry. The book names three ways the tilt can be shifted: meditation, cognitive therapy, and for some people medication, which is a matter to settle with a doctor.

cards.title: Reciprocity runs deep
cards.body: Returning favours and returning harm is one of the most dependable human instincts. It lets strangers cooperate, and it explains why a free sample makes us feel we owe something. Haidt treats it as a kind of social currency. You can use it kindly: an honest favour or a small concession often brings one back, and gossip, for all its bad name, helps a group keep track of who plays fair.

cards.title: We see others' faults, not our own
cards.body: We are skilled at spotting bias and selfishness in other people and nearly blind to them in ourselves. In a quarrel each side feels it is simply reacting to what the other one started. Haidt's suggestion is modest: find even one thing you did that added to the problem. Admitting it lowers the heat, and the other person often answers with an admission of their own.
cards.try: Think of a current disagreement and write down one way, however small, that you contributed to it.

cards.title: What changes happiness and what does not
cards.body: We adapt quickly to most improvements, such as a higher salary or a bigger home, and drift back to our usual level. Haidt points to conditions we do not fully adapt to: constant noise, a long commute, lack of control, and above all the quality of our relationships. Money spent on shortening a commute or on time with people you love may do more for you than money spent on a larger house.

cards.title: Happiness comes from between
cards.body: The book's conclusion is that happiness cannot be found by looking only inward or only outward. It arises from getting the relationships right: between you and other people, between you and your work, and between you and something larger than yourself. A person with close bonds, work that engages them and a sense of belonging to something bigger tends to find that contentment arrives without being chased.

books.title: The Righteous Mind
books.author: Jonathan Haidt
books.why: Helps you understand why decent people disagree so fiercely about politics and religion.

cards.title: Feeling first, reasons after
cards.body: Haidt argues that moral judgements arrive as quick gut reactions, and reasoning comes afterwards to defend them. Our inner thinker behaves less like a judge weighing evidence and more like a lawyer hired by our feelings. That is why a strong argument rarely changes anyone's moral view on the spot: you are answering the lawyer, while the verdict was reached somewhere else.

cards.title: We care most about looking right
cards.body: The book suggests that moral reasoning evolved to help us manage our reputation and persuade others, not to find truth alone. We are careful when someone is checking, and good at finding excuses when nobody is. This sounds bleak, but it has a useful side: people reason better when they must explain themselves to others who may disagree, so mixed company improves thinking.

cards.title: Morality has more than one taste
cards.body: Haidt compares the moral sense to a tongue with several taste receptors. He proposes six foundations: care for the vulnerable, fairness, liberty, loyalty to the group, respect for authority, and a sense of the sacred or pure. Cultures and individuals build different moral worlds from these. Someone offended by a burnt flag is responding to loyalty and sanctity, not being irrational.

cards.title: Why left and right talk past each other
cards.body: In Haidt's surveys, people on the political left rest their moral case mainly on care, fairness and liberty, while conservatives draw more evenly on all six foundations. Each side then sees the other as blind or heartless. The theory is debated among researchers and the foundations list is not settled, but it is a useful prompt: ask which value the other person is protecting.
cards.try: Take an opinion you dislike and try to name the moral value its holders believe they are defending.

cards.title: Morality binds and blinds
cards.body: Humans are selfish, Haidt says, but also deeply groupish. Shared moral beliefs let large groups of unrelated people trust each other and work together, which is a remarkable achievement. The cost is that the same beliefs make it hard to see anything good in the other team. Once a group circles around something it holds sacred, its members lose the ability to think clearly about it.

cards.title: Talk to the elephant first
cards.body: Since intuition leads and reasoning follows, persuasion starts with the relationship, not the argument. People open up to a different view when they feel liked and respected by the person offering it, and close down when attacked. If you want to be heard by a relative across the political divide, begin with what you admire or share, and show you understand their concern before you raise your own.

books.title: Emotional Intelligence
books.author: Daniel Goleman
books.why: The book that made the case that handling feelings well is a skill, and one that can be learned.

cards.title: Two minds, and the faster one
cards.body: Goleman describes us as having an emotional mind and a rational mind. The emotional one is quicker: older parts of the brain can sound an alarm before the thinking part has finished assessing the facts. He calls a full takeover an emotional hijacking. It is the moment you snap at someone and, a minute later, cannot believe what you said. The feeling was real; the response came before thought.

cards.title: Five skills, not one trait
cards.body: The book breaks emotional intelligence into five abilities: knowing what you feel, managing those feelings, motivating yourself, recognising feelings in others, and handling relationships. They build on one another, and a person can be strong in one and weak in another. Someone may read a room perfectly and still be unable to calm their own temper. Seeing them as separate skills shows where to practise.

cards.title: Notice the feeling as it happens
cards.body: Self-awareness, in Goleman's account, is the foundation for everything else. It means noticing a mood while you are in it, as if part of you stood slightly to one side: "this is anger I am feeling". That small distance is what gives you a choice. A person who cannot tell irritation from tiredness or hurt will act on the feeling without ever having examined it.
cards.try: Three times today, stop and name what you are feeling in one or two precise words.

cards.title: Venting does not drain anger
cards.body: A popular belief says that letting rage out gets rid of it. Goleman reports research suggesting the opposite: acting out anger tends to keep the body stirred up and prolongs the mood. What works better is cooling down first, for instance by going for a walk, and then questioning the thought that lit the fuse. Was the driver who cut in being hostile, or just late and careless?

cards.title: Empathy reads what is not said
cards.body: Most emotional messages travel through tone of voice, face and posture, not words. Empathy is the skill of picking these up, and it grows out of self-awareness: the better you know your own feelings, the easier it is to read someone else's. A colleague who says "fine" in a flat voice while looking away has told you two things, and the second one is the more reliable.

cards.title: What the evidence supports
cards.body: The book's lasting contribution is that emotional skills matter and can be taught, to children and adults alike. Its bolder suggestion, that these skills can count for more than IQ in how life turns out, has been criticised by later researchers as overstated, and tests of emotional intelligence vary in quality. Treat it as a strong argument for practising these skills, not as a precise measure of anyone.

books.title: Drive
books.author: Daniel H. Pink
books.why: A clear account of why rewards and punishments often fail, and what moves people instead.

cards.title: Carrots and sticks have a narrow range
cards.body: Rewards and penalties work reasonably well for simple, routine tasks where the path is clear. Pink argues that for work needing judgement or creativity they often backfire, narrowing attention and encouraging shortcuts. A bonus for the number of calls handled gets you more calls, not better help. The more thinking a task needs, the less a dangled prize helps.

cards.title: Rewards can turn play into work
cards.body: When people are paid for something they already enjoy, they may start to see it as a job and lose interest once the pay stops. The book describes research with young children who drew less in their free time after being promised a prize for drawing. Researchers still debate how large and how general this effect is, but it is a fair warning against paying a child for each book read.

cards.title: Autonomy: a say over your work
cards.body: People do better when they have some control over what they do, when, how, and with whom. Being trusted to direct yourself brings engagement, while being closely managed brings compliance at best. Even a small amount helps. A parent who lets a child choose the order of homework and chores, or a manager who sets the goal and leaves the method open, usually gets more effort, not less.
cards.try: Give someone you supervise, or a child, a real choice about how to do one task today.

cards.title: Mastery: getting better at something that matters
cards.body: The urge to improve is a strong motive in its own right. Pink notes that mastery needs tasks slightly beyond your current ability, takes effort over a long time, and is never fully reached, which is part of its pull. This is why people practise an instrument or polish code at the weekend for no pay. Work with no chance of growing feels flat however well it is rewarded.

cards.title: Purpose: serving something beyond yourself
cards.body: The third element is the sense that your effort contributes to something larger than your own gain. People who can see who benefits from their work tend to care more and last longer. Purpose need not be grand: a cleaner who thinks of the job as keeping patients safe is working with purpose. When goals are only about profit or targets, the book argues, motivation thins out.

cards.title: Pay fairly, then stop talking about money
cards.body: Pink does not say money is unimportant. If pay is too low or unfair, people think about little else. His advice is to pay enough that money is off the table, then rely on autonomy, mastery and purpose. If you do give a reward for creative work, an unexpected one after the task is finished does less harm than a prize promised in advance, since nobody was working for it.

books.title: Quiet
books.author: Susan Cain
books.why: Shows what introverts bring to work and family life, and how a loud culture overlooks it.

cards.title: Introversion is about stimulation
cards.body: Cain separates introversion from shyness. Shyness is fear of being judged. Introversion is a preference for calmer surroundings: introverts feel most alive and capable with less noise and fewer people, extroverts with more. An introvert can be warm and confident at a party and still need a quiet evening afterwards to recover. Nothing is wrong with them; their battery charges differently.

cards.title: The culture's bias toward the talker
cards.body: Cain describes an Extrovert Ideal: the belief that the best person is sociable, bold and comfortable in the spotlight. Schools seat children in groups, offices favour open plans, and the person who speaks first and most is taken to be the most capable. Yet being talkative and having good ideas are separate things. A meeting can follow the most confident voice straight past the best suggestion.

cards.title: Good work often needs solitude
cards.body: The book argues that much creative and skilled work is done alone, with long stretches of unbroken concentration. It points to research finding that people who brainstorm separately and then pool their ideas often produce more and better ones than groups thinking aloud together, where people hold back or follow the first idea raised. Collaboration matters, but it works best with privacy alongside it.
cards.try: Before your next group discussion, ask everyone to write down their ideas alone for five minutes first.

cards.title: Temperament is real but not fate
cards.body: Cain reports research following infants who reacted strongly to new sights and sounds; many grew into careful, quiet children. Sensitivity to stimulation appears to be partly inborn. But she compares temperament to a rubber band: you can stretch a good way from your starting point, though not without limit. A quiet person can learn to speak well in public and will still find it tiring.

cards.title: Stretch for what you love, then rest
cards.body: Introverts can act like extroverts for the sake of work or people they care deeply about; a reserved teacher can light up a lecture hall. Cain draws on the idea that we can act out of character in the service of projects that matter to us, but that doing so has a cost. The answer is to plan recovery: a quiet lunch, a walk alone, a short gap between meetings.
cards.try: Look at tomorrow's schedule and put one short quiet break after the most social part of the day.

cards.title: Living with the other type
cards.body: Introverts and extroverts often pair up and then misread each other. One wants to talk a conflict through at once, the other needs to withdraw and think, and each takes the other's style as aggression or coldness. Cain's advice is to name the difference. For a quiet child, it means introducing new situations gradually and never labelling them as shy in front of others.

books.title: The Body Keeps the Score
books.author: Bessel van der Kolk
books.why: An influential account of how overwhelming experiences can stay with a person in body as well as mind.

cards.title: Trauma is not only a story
cards.body: Van der Kolk's central claim is that trauma is not just a memory of something bad. It can leave the body's alarm system set too high, so that a person reacts to ordinary life as if the danger were still present: tense muscles, a racing heart, sleep that does not restore. This helps explain why someone can know perfectly well that they are safe now and still not feel it.

cards.title: Reliving instead of remembering
cards.body: An ordinary memory is a story with a beginning and an end that we know lies in the past. The book describes how traumatic memories can instead return as fragments: a smell, a sound, a wave of terror, as though it were happening again. A slammed door or a certain tone of voice can set it off. Understanding this can replace "why am I overreacting?" with a kinder and more accurate question.

cards.title: Early adversity casts a long shadow
cards.body: The book draws on research linking abuse, neglect and chaos in childhood to higher rates of physical and mental illness decades later. A child cannot leave a frightening home, so the growing brain and body adapt to constant threat. Van der Kolk argues that many adult difficulties are better understood as these old adaptations than as character flaws, which changes how we look at ourselves and others.

cards.title: Safety with other people comes first
cards.body: Feeling truly safe with another person is, in van der Kolk's view, the base on which recovery is built. Being seen and heard by someone steady calms the body in a way that reasoning alone cannot. This is why isolation makes things worse, and why patient, reliable company from a friend or relative matters even when they have no idea what to say.

cards.title: Many roads, uneven evidence
cards.body: The author argues that talking is valuable but sometimes not enough, and describes approaches that work through the body, such as yoga, a therapy called EMDR, and others. The evidence is uneven: some trauma therapies are well tested, others much less, and critics say the book overstates parts of its brain science. It is not a treatment guide. Anyone struggling should work with a qualified professional.

cards.title: Learning to notice the body again
cards.body: People who have been overwhelmed often cope by tuning out physical sensation altogether, which also dulls pleasure and the ordinary signals of hunger, tiredness and ease. The book describes gently rebuilding the ability to notice what the body feels as a part of regaining a sense of control. If paying attention to your body brings distress and not calm, that is a reason to do it with professional support.

books.title: Obedience to Authority
books.author: Stanley Milgram
books.why: The classic and troubling study of how far ordinary people will go when someone in charge tells them to.

cards.title: The experiment
cards.body: Milgram invited ordinary adults to what they were told was a study of learning. An experimenter in a lab coat instructed each one to give a "learner" in the next room a stronger electric shock for every wrong answer. The shocks were fake and the learner was an actor, but the volunteers were not told. In the best-known version about two thirds continued to the highest level on the machine.

cards.title: From own person to instrument
cards.body: Milgram's explanation is that people entering a hierarchy can shift into seeing themselves as carrying out someone else's wishes. In that state they feel responsible to the authority for doing the job well, but not responsible for what the job does. "I was only following the procedure" is the everyday form. The shift is easy to slide into and hard to notice from the inside.
cards.try: The next time you carry out an instruction you feel uneasy about, ask yourself: who answers for the result?

cards.title: The setting decided more than character
cards.body: Milgram ran many variations, and obedience rose and fell with the arrangement. It dropped when the victim was in the same room, when the experimenter gave orders by telephone, and most sharply when volunteers saw others refuse. He found it hard to predict from personality who would stop. The lesson he drew is that the details of a situation can outweigh the kind of person you believe you are.

cards.title: One small step at a time
cards.body: The shocks rose in small steps, each only a little stronger than the one before. Having agreed to the last step, a person found it hard to explain why this next one was different, and stopping meant admitting that the earlier steps were wrong too. Many harmful courses of action work this way, at work and elsewhere: no single step feels like the moment to refuse.

cards.title: They obeyed without wanting to
cards.body: Most volunteers did not enjoy it. Milgram describes people sweating, protesting, pleading with the experimenter, and continuing anyway. Breaking off meant openly defying a polite, confident person and disrupting the occasion, and that social awkwardness proved surprisingly powerful. Feeling that something is wrong is not the same as acting on it; the second takes practice.

cards.title: Read it with care
cards.body: The studies caused real distress and would not pass an ethics review today. Later researchers who examined the archives found the procedure was less uniform than the book suggests and that a number of volunteers doubted the shocks were real. Partial repeats that stopped at a lower shock level did find similar rates of compliance. The broad point survives; the exact figures deserve caution.

books.title: The Lucifer Effect
books.author: Philip Zimbardo
books.why: A forceful, and contested, argument that situations and systems can lead ordinary people into cruelty.

cards.title: Bad barrels, not only bad apples
cards.body: When people behave terribly we usually blame their character. Zimbardo asks us to look also at the barrel: the situation they were put in, and the system of leaders, rules and incentives that built it. This does not excuse anyone. But if only the individuals are punished and the conditions stay the same, the next group placed in those conditions is likely to behave in much the same way.

cards.title: The prison study and its problems
cards.body: The book centres on Zimbardo's 1971 study in which students were assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock jail; he reports that guards turned abusive within days. This study is now heavily disputed. Records show the guards were encouraged to be tough, some participants say they were acting, and a later attempt to repeat it had different results. It is best read as a vivid demonstration, not proof.

cards.title: Anonymity loosens restraint
cards.body: Zimbardo argues that people act more harshly when they feel unidentifiable and part of a mass: in uniform, masked, hidden in a crowd or behind a screen name. Feeling personally seen and answerable works the other way. The practical point holds up in everyday life: online comments turn crueller when nobody knows who wrote them, and people soften when addressed by name.

cards.title: Labels that remove the human
cards.body: Cruelty becomes easier once the target is described as less than a person: a number, a category, an insult for a whole group. The label lets ordinary moral feeling switch off. Zimbardo treats this as an early warning sign in any group. Listen to how an organisation or a movement talks about outsiders; the words usually change before the behaviour does.

cards.title: Small steps and silent witnesses
cards.body: The book lists the ingredients that draw decent people into harm: a first small step, a plausible justification, a gradual increase, responsibility spread so thin that nobody owns it, and people who watch and say nothing. Zimbardo applies this to the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib, arguing that those who created the conditions shared the blame with the soldiers who were convicted.

cards.title: Heroes are ordinary too
cards.body: If situations can pull ordinary people toward harm, Zimbardo says, they can also call out ordinary courage. Most people who refuse an unjust order or speak up are not special; they acted at the moment that counted. He suggests preparing in advance: be willing to say "I was wrong", notice when you are being hurried, and keep a sense of personal responsibility even inside a group.
cards.try: Decide now on one line you will not cross at work, so that you recognise the moment if it ever comes.

books.title: Mistakes Were Made (but Not by Me)
books.author: Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson
books.why: Explains why it is so hard to admit being wrong, and how self-justification quietly runs our lives.

cards.title: The discomfort that drives excuses
cards.body: Holding two ideas that clash, such as "I am a sensible, decent person" and "I just did something foolish or unkind", is unpleasant. The authors explain that we ease the discomfort not by changing our view of ourselves but by adjusting the story: it was not so bad, they deserved it, anyone would have done it. The excuse arrives so fast that we believe it. Self-justification is not lying to others; it is lying to ourselves.

cards.title: The pyramid of choice
cards.body: Picture two people at the top of a pyramid, close together, facing the same temptation. One gives in slightly, the other resists slightly. Each then justifies the choice, and each justification makes the next step in the same direction easier. By the bottom they stand far apart, each sure the other is a different kind of person. Big moral differences often begin as small, almost accidental first steps.

cards.title: Memory edits in our favour
cards.body: Memory, the authors argue, works less like a recording and more like a biographer on our side. Over time we recall our past views as closer to our present ones, our motives as better, and the other person's behaviour as worse. Two siblings can remember the same family quarrel with each cast as the reasonable one. A confident, detailed memory feels like proof, but it is not.
cards.try: Ask a relative or old friend how they remember an event you both lived through, and just listen to the differences.

cards.title: Everyone is biased except me
cards.body: We readily see how money, loyalty or pride bend other people's judgement and assume our own view is simply how things are. The book shows professionals of every kind, from doctors to prosecutors, insisting that gifts or first impressions could not possibly sway them. Since the bias cannot be felt from inside, the only protection is outside: people and procedures allowed to check us.

cards.title: Why admitting error gets harder
cards.body: The more time, money, effort or reputation we have put into a decision, the more painful it is to admit it was wrong, and the harder we defend it. The authors describe investigators who cling to their first suspect even after new evidence clears that person. At home it is the same: the longer a couple has blamed each other, the more each has invested in being the wronged one.

cards.title: Separate the mistake from the self
cards.body: The book's remedy is to hold both thoughts at once: I am a capable, decent person, and I got this wrong. Kept together, they let you fix the error without tearing yourself down or explaining it away. People generally respect a plain admission far more than we fear. "I made a mistake, here is what I will do about it" tends to end an argument that excuses would have prolonged.
cards.try: Find one thing you got wrong this week and say so plainly to the person affected, with no "but" attached.

books.title: The Social Animal
books.author: Elliot Aronson
books.why: A warm and readable tour of social psychology by one of the field's best teachers.

cards.title: Odd behaviour is not always an odd person
cards.body: Aronson offers a first rule for understanding people: strange or even shocking behaviour does not prove that the person is strange. Before judging character, look at the pressures of the situation they were in. The colleague who went along with a bad decision may have been facing a room of nodding heads. This habit makes you fairer to others and more alert to the pressures that act on you too.

cards.title: The pull to go along
cards.body: In a classic study that Aronson describes, people asked to judge the length of lines often agreed with a group that was obviously wrong, on a notable share of the trials. They knew what they saw and doubted it, or did not want to stand out. The encouraging part: when just one other person gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply. A single ally makes independence far easier.
cards.try: In your next meeting, if you privately disagree, say so once. You may be the ally someone else was waiting for.

cards.title: Three depths of influence
cards.body: People go along for different reasons, and Aronson separates three. Compliance is doing something to gain a reward or avoid trouble; it lasts only while someone is watching. Identification is doing it to be like a person we admire. Internalisation is doing it because we have come to believe it is right, and only this one lasts by itself. A child who tidies up only when threatened has learned the first kind.

cards.title: We love what we suffered for
cards.body: When we go through effort or discomfort to get something, we tend to rate it more highly afterwards, since admitting it was not worth the trouble would make us feel foolish. Aronson's own research found that people who went through an unpleasant initiation to join a dull group liked the group more. It explains our loyalty to hard-won clubs, courses and jobs, deserved or not.

cards.title: Cooperation dissolves prejudice
cards.body: Simply putting hostile groups in the same room does little. Aronson helped develop the jigsaw classroom, where each child holds one piece of a lesson and the group can only succeed if everyone teaches their part. Needing one another changed how the children saw each other. The same principle applies at work and at home: a shared goal that requires everyone does more than lectures about getting along.

cards.title: What makes us like someone
cards.body: Aronson reviews what draws people together: being nearby, being similar, and above all being liked in return. One finding from his own lab is that a highly capable person can become more likeable after a small blunder, such as spilling a drink, because it makes them seem human. It does not work for someone seen as mediocre. You do not need to appear flawless to be liked.

books.title: The Invisible Gorilla
books.author: Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons
books.why: Six everyday illusions about our own minds, each shown with memorable and well-tested examples.

cards.title: We see far less than we think
cards.body: In the authors' best-known study, people counting basketball passes in a video often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walk through the scene; about half missed it. We experience a rich, complete view of the world, but we only take in what we attend to. The rest can pass unseen while our eyes point straight at it. This is why talking on a phone while driving is risky even with both hands on the wheel.
cards.try: On your next drive or walk in traffic, put the phone fully out of reach before you set off.

cards.title: Vivid memories can be wrong
cards.body: We assume a detailed, confident memory must be accurate. The authors show that memories of even dramatic events shift over time: details are added, borrowed from other people's accounts or reshaped, while confidence stays high. Two people can sincerely recall the same conversation in opposite ways. A strong feeling of certainty tells you about the feeling, not about the facts.

cards.title: Confidence is not competence
cards.body: We tend to trust the person who sounds sure: the firm witness, the decisive doctor, the assured candidate. But confidence is partly a personality trait and only loosely tied to accuracy. The authors add that people with little skill in an area are often the least aware of it. A doctor who checks a reference book in front of you may be the better doctor, even though it feels less reassuring.

cards.title: We know less than we feel we know
cards.body: Most people believe they understand how familiar things work until they are asked to explain them step by step. The feeling of familiarity passes for knowledge. The same illusion makes us underestimate how long projects will take, since we picture the plan and not the snags. Trying to explain a thing in detail is a quick, humbling test of what you really know.
cards.try: Pick an everyday object, such as a zip or a toilet flush, and try to explain exactly how it works.

cards.title: Seeing causes that are not there
cards.body: Our minds are built to find patterns and to assume that when one thing follows another, the first caused the second. We are also moved far more by a single vivid story than by dull statistics. The authors use these habits to explain how health scares spread: one family's convincing account of what happened after a treatment can outweigh careful studies of many thousands of people.

cards.title: No quick route to a better brain
cards.body: The last illusion is the belief that we have large untapped mental powers which a simple trick can release. The authors examine claims that listening to classical music makes babies smarter, or that brain-training games sharpen the whole mind, and find the evidence weak. Practice mainly improves the specific thing you practise. Real improvement comes slowly, through effort in the skill itself.

books.title: Noise
books.author: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass R. Sunstein
books.why: Points to a large and overlooked source of error: judgements that ought to match and do not.

cards.title: Bias and noise are different errors
cards.body: Picture a team shooting at a target. If every shot lands low and left, that is bias: a consistent lean. If the shots scatter all over, that is noise. Bias gets the attention, but the authors argue that noise does as much damage. Whenever two doctors, judges or managers look at the same case and reach very different conclusions, somebody is being treated unfairly and money is being wasted.

cards.title: There is more of it than anyone expects
cards.body: When organisations test for it, by giving the same case to several of their own professionals, the spread of answers is usually far wider than their leaders guessed. The authors report this in settings as varied as court sentences, insurance quotes and medical diagnoses. It stays hidden because each case is decided once, by one person, and nobody sees the answer a colleague would have given.

cards.title: You are not the same judge all day
cards.body: Noise is not only between people. The same person decides differently depending on mood, tiredness, the weather, or what case came just before. The authors call this occasion noise. It means your judgement on a Friday afternoon is one draw from a range of judgements you might have made. For a decision that matters, sleeping on it and deciding again is a way of asking yourself twice.
cards.try: For one important decision this week, write down your answer today, then decide again tomorrow before looking.

cards.title: Decision hygiene
cards.body: Washing your hands prevents infections without your ever knowing which ones. The authors propose similar habits for judgement: routines that reduce error in general, without needing to know which error was avoided. They are unglamorous and come with no moment of triumph, which is why they are neglected. The following cards describe the main ones.

cards.title: Judge separately, then combine
cards.body: Averaging several independent judgements cancels out much of the scatter, but only if they are truly independent. Once people hear each other, they drift together and the first or loudest opinion wins. So collect views before discussion, not after. In hiring, this means each interviewer scores the candidate alone, on agreed qualities, before anyone compares notes.
cards.try: Before your next group decision, ask everyone to write their own estimate or vote before any discussion.

cards.title: Break it up and hold back the gut
cards.body: Complex judgements improve when they are split into separate parts, each assessed on its merits, with the overall impression delayed until the end. A quick early impression tends to colour everything after it. The authors also note that simple rules and formulas often match or beat expert judgement, mainly because a rule gives the same answer to the same case every time.

books.title: Misbehaving
books.author: Richard H. Thaler
books.why: The story of how economists were persuaded, slowly, that real people do not behave like their models.

cards.title: The things that should not matter
cards.body: Standard economic theory assumed people weigh costs and benefits coolly and consistently. Thaler spent his career collecting cases where they plainly do not, and calls the causes supposedly irrelevant factors: the way a price is described, what we already own, what feels fair. The theory says these should not change behaviour. They do, predictably, and so any good model of people must include them.

cards.title: Losing hurts more than gaining pleases
cards.body: Thaler found that people given an ordinary object, such as a mug, would only sell it for roughly twice what others were willing to pay for one. Nothing about the mug had changed except who owned it. Giving something up registers as a loss, and losses weigh more heavily than gains of the same size. It is why clearing a cupboard is hard and why a refused refund stings more than a missed discount.

cards.title: Money wears labels
cards.body: In theory money is all the same. In practice we sort it into mental accounts: rent, holidays, fun, savings. This helps with budgeting but leads to odd behaviour, such as keeping savings at low interest while carrying expensive card debt, or spending a tax refund freely because it feels like a bonus. Thaler notes that gamblers treat winnings as the house's money and risk it more readily.
cards.try: Look at any windfall or "fun money" you have, and ask what you would do with it if it had arrived as salary.

cards.title: Money already spent is gone
cards.body: Having paid for something, we feel we must use it, even when using it no longer does us any good. People drive through bad weather to an event because the ticket was expensive, or finish a meal they are not enjoying. The money is spent either way; the only real question is what you want to do now. Thaler shows that even people who teach this principle fall for it.
cards.try: Is there something you keep doing only because you already paid for it? Decide afresh as if it had been free.

cards.title: The planner and the doer
cards.body: Thaler describes each of us as two selves: a far-sighted planner and a doer who lives in the present. The planner cannot simply overrule the doer, so it sets up rules and removes temptations in advance. He tells of taking a bowl of nuts away from dinner guests who kept eating them before the meal, and being thanked for it. Having fewer options within reach can leave us better off.

cards.title: Fairness has a price
cards.body: People will give up money to punish what they see as unfair treatment. Thaler's research with colleagues found that most people think it wrong for a shop to raise the price of snow shovels the morning after a storm, although standard theory sees nothing odd in it. Businesses that ignore this lose goodwill. Any dealing, from splitting a bill to setting a rent, goes better when it also looks fair.

books.title: The Paradox of Choice
books.author: Barry Schwartz
books.why: Argues that beyond a certain point more options make us less satisfied, and shows how to cope.

cards.title: When more is less
cards.body: Some choice is essential to wellbeing, and Schwartz does not dispute it. His claim is that as options multiply, the effort of deciding grows, we put decisions off, and we enjoy the result less. He cites a well-known study in which shoppers bought more jam from a small display than a large one. Later attempts to repeat such findings have had mixed results, so choice overload seems real in some conditions, not all.

cards.title: Maximisers and satisficers
cards.body: A maximiser needs to be sure they have picked the best possible option and so must examine them all. A satisficer has standards, sometimes high ones, and stops at the first option that meets them. Schwartz reports that maximisers may get slightly better outcomes but feel worse about them, because they keep wondering about the ones they did not choose. In most areas of life, good enough really is.
cards.try: For one decision today, set your criteria first and take the first option that meets them.

cards.title: Every option you reject costs something
cards.body: Choosing one thing means giving up the appealing features of the others. With two options the loss is small. With thirty, the combined attractions of everything passed over can outweigh the pleasure of the one chosen. This is why a long menu can leave you eyeing your neighbour's plate. Fewer alternatives mean fewer imagined losses to subtract from what you have.

cards.title: Regret, before and after
cards.body: The more options there were, the easier it is to imagine that a different one would have been better, and to blame yourself. Fear of that regret can also stop people choosing at all, as when a pension form sits unfilled for years. Schwartz observes that regret is sharpest when a result was nearly good and when the choice was ours alone, which abundant choice makes more common.

cards.title: High expectations spoil good results
cards.body: When there are hundreds of options, we expect that one of them must be perfect. A result that is merely good then feels like a disappointment, and since we did the choosing, it feels like our fault. Schwartz argues that the secret of contentment is partly modest expectations. People with few options are pleasantly surprised more often than people who assumed the ideal was available.

cards.title: Choose when to choose
cards.body: Schwartz's advice is to save careful choosing for the few decisions that matter and use rules and habits for the rest: the same breakfast, two shops and no more. Treat decisions as final where you can, since revisiting them breeds doubt. Practise noticing what is good about what you chose. Limits you set for yourself, he argues, can be a relief and not a loss of freedom.
cards.try: Pick one recurring small decision, such as lunch or what to watch, and settle it with a simple rule for a week.

books.title: Learned Optimism
books.author: Martin E. P. Seligman
books.why: Shows that the way you explain setbacks to yourself is a habit, and one that can be changed.

cards.title: Helplessness can be learned
cards.body: Seligman's early research found that animals, and people, who faced unpleasant events they could not control often stopped trying, even later when escape was easy. They had learned that nothing they did mattered. He saw in this a model for the passivity of depression. He and his colleagues later refined the theory, concluding that what is learned is the sense of control, but the practical insight stands.

cards.title: How you explain bad events
cards.body: What separates optimists from pessimists, Seligman argues, is their habit of explaining misfortune. He looks at three questions. Is the cause permanent or temporary? Does it spoil everything or only one area? Is it all my fault or partly circumstance? After a failed interview the pessimist thinks "I always mess up, I am hopeless at everything", the optimist "that one went badly; I was underprepared".
cards.try: Write down how you explained your last setback, and check it for the words "always", "never" and "everything".

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: In Seligman's account, people who explain setbacks as permanent, all-embracing and personal give up sooner and are more prone to low mood, while those who see them as temporary and specific keep going. He reports this pattern in classrooms, sports teams and sales forces. Persistence after failure often decides the result, so the explanation you give yourself affects what happens next.

cards.title: Catch the belief between event and feeling
cards.body: Seligman borrows a tool from cognitive therapy. Something bad happens (adversity), you interpret it (belief), and the interpretation, not the event, produces the feeling and what you do (consequence). A friend does not return your call; if you believe "she is tired of me", you feel hurt and withdraw. Writing down the three parts makes visible the middle step that normally goes by too fast to see.

cards.title: Argue with yourself
cards.body: Once you have caught a pessimistic belief, treat it as you would an accusation from someone else and dispute it. What is the evidence? Is there another explanation? If it is true, how bad are the consequences really? Is the belief any use to me? Most of us defend ourselves well against unfair criticism from others and never think to do it against our own. This is a skill that improves with practice.
cards.try: Take one gloomy thought from today and write out the evidence against it, as if defending a friend.

cards.title: Optimism with its eyes open
cards.body: Seligman does not recommend optimism everywhere. Where being wrong would be costly, such as a safety decision or a large financial risk, a cautious and even pessimistic view is wiser. He calls the goal flexible optimism: choosing the hopeful explanation when it helps you persist and the sober one when the stakes demand it. The book is not a substitute for treatment; lasting depression calls for professional help.

books.title: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
books.author: Oliver Sacks
books.why: Humane case histories that show how much of who we are depends on the workings of the brain.

cards.title: Seeing without recognising
cards.body: The title case is a gifted music teacher who could see perfectly well but had lost the ability to recognise what he saw. He could describe a glove's shape in detail without knowing what it was, and faces meant nothing to him. He got through the day by humming, turning dressing and eating into a kind of song. Sacks uses him to show that seeing and making sense of what is seen are separate jobs in the brain.

cards.title: The man stuck in one year
cards.body: Sacks describes a former sailor whose memory for new events had been destroyed. He believed it was still the 1940s and that he was a young man, and forgot each conversation within moments. Sacks asks whether such a person has lost his self. Yet in chapel, in music and in the garden he became calm, attentive and whole. Something of a person, Sacks concludes, lives deeper than memory.

cards.title: The sense you never notice
cards.body: One patient lost, almost overnight, the sense that tells us where our limbs are without looking. She felt as if she had no body, and had to learn to move by watching each hand and foot. Sacks uses her to draw attention to this hidden sense, which works so silently that we never think of it, yet it underlies the feeling of being at home in one's own body.

cards.title: Too much, not only too little
cards.body: Neurology usually talks about loss. Sacks devotes a section to excess: too much energy, impulse or imagination. He writes of a man with Tourette's syndrome whose tics made life hard, but whose quickness also fed his wit and his drumming. Medication calmed him and dulled him. In the end he took it during the working week and went without at weekends, choosing for himself between two ways of being.

cards.title: Ask what the person can do
cards.body: Tests measure what is missing. Sacks writes about a young woman who failed them badly, and was clumsy and lost in ordinary tasks, yet was composed and fluent when listening to stories, in nature, and later on stage in a theatre group. She made it clear that drills did nothing for her; she needed something that gave her days a pattern. The point reaches beyond medicine: people are often best understood through what brings them together, not what they lack.
cards.try: Think of someone you find difficult or limited, and name one setting in which they are at their best.

cards.title: The patient is a person with a story
cards.body: Running through the book is Sacks's method. He does not stop at naming a condition; he asks how this individual lives with it, adapts to it and holds on to an identity. A diagnosis says what a person has, and a story shows who they are. It is a useful habit for anyone caring for an ill or elderly relative: learn the condition, and then keep paying attention to the person.

books.title: Behave
books.author: Robert M. Sapolsky
books.why: A sweeping account of why we act as we do, from the second before to millions of years before.

cards.title: No single cause
cards.body: Sapolsky's method is to take one act, kind or cruel, and ask what explains it. What happened in the brain a second before? What sights or stresses in the minutes before set that up? What hormones in the hours and days before? What childhood, what culture, what evolutionary history? Each level is part of the answer. Whenever someone says a behaviour is caused by a gene, a hormone or an upbringing alone, be doubtful.

cards.title: The slow-maturing brake
cards.body: The frontal cortex is the part of the brain that lets us take the difficult course when it is the better one: wait, hold back, think of consequences. It is the last region to mature, not finishing until the mid-twenties. That goes a long way to explaining adolescent risk-taking and intensity. It is less a failure of character than a brain whose brakes are still being fitted.

cards.title: Hormones turn up what is already there
cards.body: Popular belief says testosterone causes aggression and oxytocin causes love. Sapolsky shows it is subtler. Testosterone mostly amplifies tendencies that are already present and depends heavily on the social setting. Oxytocin strengthens bonds with those we count as our own, and can at the same time sharpen coldness toward outsiders. Hormones do not issue orders; they change the volume.

cards.title: Us and Them, in a blink
cards.body: We sort people into "us" and "them" within a fraction of a second, on cues as slight as a face or an accent, and feel differently about each. Sapolsky stresses that the categories are remarkably easy to redraw: a shared team, a shared task, or learning one personal detail about someone can shift them. We cannot stop the sorting, but we have a say in who ends up counted as "us".
cards.try: With someone you feel is "not your sort", find out one ordinary personal thing, such as what they like to eat.

cards.title: Stress makes us worse
cards.body: Short bursts of stress sharpen us. Sustained stress, Sapolsky explains, weakens the frontal cortex's control and strengthens the brain's fear responses. Under it we fall back on habit, judge risks poorly, become more self-centred and are more likely to take things out on those nearby. If you have a serious decision to make or a difficult talk to have, the state you are in when you do it matters.
cards.try: If you are tense, put off one difficult conversation until after you have eaten, moved about or slept.

cards.title: Genes work through surroundings
cards.body: Genes do not dictate behaviour. Their effects depend on the environment in which they act, so the same gene can have different consequences in different settings, and none at all in some. For Sapolsky the useful question is not what a gene does in general, but what it does in a given setting. He draws from this, and from the whole book, a case for humility in judging others.

books.title: On Becoming a Person
books.author: Carl R. Rogers
books.why: A founder of humanistic psychology on how people grow, and what kind of listening helps them do it.

cards.title: Three things that help a person grow
cards.body: From years as a therapist Rogers concluded that people change in a relationship with three qualities. The helper is genuine, not hiding behind a role. The helper accepts the other person warmly without conditions. And the helper works to understand the other's world from the inside. He believed these matter in any relationship, between parent and child or teacher and pupil as much as in therapy.

cards.title: People lean toward growth
cards.body: Rogers held that every person has a built-in tendency to develop and mature, much as a plant grows toward light. It can be buried under fear and defensiveness, but in the right climate it reappears. So the helper's job is not to fix or direct but to provide the conditions. Parents may recognise this: a child who feels safe and accepted often finds the way forward without being pushed.

cards.title: Acceptance comes before change
cards.body: Rogers noticed something that seems backwards. As long as we fight what we are, insisting we should not feel angry or afraid, we stay stuck. When we can admit the feeling as it is, movement begins. Accepting is not approving or giving up; it is seeing clearly what is there. The same holds for other people: someone who feels accepted is far freer to change than someone who feels judged.
cards.try: Name one thing about yourself that you usually argue with, and for today simply acknowledge that it is so.

cards.title: Listen to understand, not to judge
cards.body: Our first reaction to what another person says, Rogers observed, is to evaluate it: agree, disagree, approve, correct. That reflex is the main barrier to communication. He proposed a rule for arguments: before making your own point, restate the other person's view accurately enough that they agree you have got it. It is harder than it sounds, and it usually takes the heat out of the dispute.
cards.try: In your next disagreement, say back the other person's point in your own words before you answer it.

cards.title: Dropping the mask
cards.body: Rogers describes a common direction in people who are growing. They move away from pretending and from living by what others expect, and toward trusting their own experience as a guide. They come to see themselves as a process that keeps unfolding, not a finished product. For Rogers a good life is a direction of travel, with more openness and more feeling, including the painful kind.

books.title: Motivation and Personality
books.author: Abraham H. Maslow
books.why: The source of the famous hierarchy of needs, and a richer and more careful book than the pyramid suggests.

cards.title: Needs come in a rough order
cards.body: Maslow proposed that human needs fall into groups that tend to press on us in sequence: bodily needs such as food and sleep, then safety, then love and belonging, then esteem, and finally the need to fulfil one's potential. The more basic ones usually demand attention first. A person who is hungry or frightened has little room to think about anything else, however talented they are.

cards.title: A met need stops pushing
cards.body: One of Maslow's sharper observations is that a satisfied need no longer motivates. Once you are fed, food stops organising your thoughts, and something else takes its place. This is why people are rarely content for long: we are, he says, wanting creatures. It also explains why a pay rise delights briefly and then fades, while a missing sense of belonging or respect starts to ache.
cards.try: Ask yourself which need is loudest for you right now: rest, security, company, respect, or growth.

cards.title: It was never a rigid ladder
cards.body: The neat pyramid found in textbooks is not in the book, and Maslow did not claim one level must be complete before the next begins. He wrote that most people are partly satisfied and partly unsatisfied at every level at once, and he listed exceptions, such as people who put a cause above their own safety. Later research supports the importance of these needs but not a fixed order.

cards.title: Becoming what you can be
cards.body: At the top Maslow placed self-actualisation: the desire to become fully what one is capable of being. A musician needs to make music and a teacher to teach, or a restlessness sets in even when every other need is met. It takes a different form in each person and has nothing to do with fame. A discontent that appears when life is comfortable may be this need speaking.

cards.title: A portrait of people at their best
cards.body: Maslow studied people he judged to be unusually healthy and fulfilled. He found they tended to see reality clearly, accept themselves and others, focus on problems outside themselves, value privacy, keep a few deep friendships and hold a kindly sense of humour. He admitted his method was informal and his sample hand-picked, so this is a thoughtful sketch, not a scientific finding.

cards.title: Study health, not only illness
cards.body: Maslow complained that psychology had learned about human nature mainly from the troubled, and so knew a great deal about our weaknesses and little about our strengths. He argued for studying the healthiest people to learn what humans can be. The study of wellbeing that grew up decades later owes him this starting point, and his question is still a good one to ask of yourself.
cards.try: Write down one thing that is going right in your life, and what it shows you are good at.

books.title: The Nature of Prejudice
books.author: Gordon W. Allport
books.why: The founding study of prejudice, still the clearest explanation of where it comes from and what reduces it.

cards.title: Prejudice grows from ordinary thinking
cards.body: Allport begins with an awkward fact: the mind has to sort things into categories to cope with the world, and it does the same with people. Categories save effort and are often good enough. Prejudice starts from this normal habit. It is an overgeneralised belief about a group, joined to a feeling about them, and applied to an individual who has not been looked at as an individual.

cards.title: A mistake versus a prejudice
cards.body: Everyone makes hasty judgements. Allport's test of true prejudice is what happens when contrary evidence arrives. A simple error gets corrected. A prejudice resists: the person admits that this one member of the group is different, treats them as an exception, and keeps the general belief intact. "Some of my best friends are..." is the sound of a category being protected.
cards.try: Think of a group you have a fixed view of. When did you last meet someone who did not fit, and what did you do with that?

cards.title: From words to violence
cards.body: Allport laid out a scale of how prejudice is acted on, each step making the next more thinkable. It starts with hostile talk among the like-minded, moves to avoiding the group, then to excluding them from jobs, housing or rights, then to physical attack, and at the extreme to mass killing. Most prejudice never goes beyond talk. But the scale is the reason "only jokes" deserve attention.

cards.title: Loving your own need not mean hating others
cards.body: We all belong to in-groups: family, region, faith, profession. They give us identity and security. Allport argued that attachment to one's own group does not require hostility to outsiders; many people are devoted to their own without ill will to anyone. Hostility is an added ingredient, often supplied when a group feels threatened or when someone gains from stirring it.

cards.title: Blaming a convenient target
cards.body: When people are frustrated by things they cannot control or confront, such as hard times or a powerful boss, the anger tends to land on someone safer. Allport describes how minorities, being visible and unable to hit back, are made to carry the blame for problems they did not cause. It is worth noticing in public life when a complicated difficulty is suddenly pinned on one group.

cards.title: Contact, under the right conditions
cards.body: Allport's most influential idea is that prejudice falls when members of different groups meet on equal footing, work together toward a shared goal, and have the backing of law, custom or those in authority. Casual or unequal contact can make things worse. Decades of later research have largely supported him. A mixed sports team or a joint work project does what speeches cannot.
cards.try: Find one shared task, at work or in your neighbourhood, that you could do alongside someone from a different background.

books.title: The Crowd
books.author: Gustave Le Bon
books.why: The first famous theory of how people change in a mass, still worth reading with a critical eye.

cards.title: A crowd is more than its members
cards.body: Le Bon's main claim is that people gathered around a shared focus can form what he called a psychological crowd, whose feelings and actions differ from what each person would feel or do alone. Individual judgement recedes and a common mood takes over. You may have felt a version of this in a stadium, at a rally or a festival, when you were carried along by something larger.

cards.title: Numbers bring a feeling of power
cards.body: In a mass, Le Bon argued, a person feels anonymous and therefore less answerable for what they do, and at the same time senses an almost unlimited strength in the numbers around them. Impulses that would be held in check alone are released. The same mechanism can be seen today when someone posts in an online pile-on what they would never say face to face.

cards.title: Feelings spread like a contagion
cards.body: Le Bon held that emotions and actions pass rapidly from person to person in a crowd, and that people in this state are highly open to suggestion. Fear turns to panic, enthusiasm to frenzy. He leaned on the medical ideas of his day, which have not lasted, but the observation that moods travel through groups is familiar to anyone who has caught a room's laughter or tension.
cards.try: The next time a group's mood sweeps you up, pause and ask what you would think if you were on your own.

cards.title: Images persuade crowds, not arguments
cards.body: According to Le Bon, crowds do not reason their way to conclusions. They respond to vivid images, simple claims and strong feeling. He named three tools by which ideas take hold of them: plain assertion without proof, constant repetition, and contagion from person to person. More than a century later, advertising and political slogans still use exactly these three.

cards.title: The prestige of leaders
cards.body: Le Bon wrote that crowds instinctively place themselves under a leader, and that the leader's hold depends less on reasoning than on prestige: an aura that stops people from judging critically. Prestige can come from position, wealth or reputation, or from personal force. He noted that it is fragile and tends to collapse once it is openly questioned or the leader fails.

cards.title: What modern research says
cards.body: Le Bon was an observer writing in alarm at the politics of his time, not an experimenter, and the book carries prejudices about class, race and women that are plainly unacceptable. Modern studies of crowds find that they are often orderly, cooperative and self-policing, and that people in them act on shared identity and values, not blind impulse. Read him for the questions he raised, not as settled fact.

books.title: The True Believer
books.author: Eric Hoffer
books.why: A short, sharp reflection on why people give themselves over to mass movements of every kind.

cards.title: All fanaticisms are related
cards.body: Hoffer's starting point is that mass movements, whether religious, nationalist or revolutionary, differ in doctrine but attract the same sort of mind and use it in similar ways. Someone ripe for one cause is ripe for others, which is why converts sometimes swing between opposite extremes. To understand a movement's grip, he suggests, look less at what it preaches and more at what joining does for the person.

cards.title: An escape from the self
cards.body: People who are at peace with their lives, Hoffer argues, rarely want to overturn the world. The most willing recruits are those who feel their own lives are spoiled or meaningless. A cause offers them a way to shed an unwanted self and be reborn as part of something large and certain. On this view, passionate devotion to a cause can be a way of not having to face oneself.
cards.try: Think of the cause or group you feel most strongly about, and ask honestly what belonging to it gives you.

cards.title: Who is most easily drawn in
cards.body: Hoffer observes that the destitute, absorbed in daily survival, seldom rebel. More restless are those who have recently lost their footing or have tasted something better and want more. He adds misfits who have not found their place, people who are simply bored, and those weighed down by guilt. The common thread is frustration: a sense that the present life is not worth keeping.

cards.title: The future against the present
cards.body: Movements, Hoffer writes, run down the present and fix all hope on a glorious time to come, or a glorious past to be restored. If today is worthless there is nothing to lose by sacrificing it. This is how ordinary people are brought to accept hardship and risk. A group that keeps telling you everything around you is rotten and only its future is real deserves a second look.

cards.title: Unity needs an enemy
cards.body: Hoffer holds that hatred is the most reliable cement for a movement. A cause can do without anything to worship, he suggests, but it cannot do without a villain: an enemy to blame for all that is wrong. The enemy is best when it is single, vivid and close at hand. When a group defines itself mainly by who it is against, that tells you how it holds its members together.

cards.title: What kind of book this is
cards.body: Hoffer was a dock worker and self-taught thinker, and this is a book of observations and striking generalisations, not research. It gives no data, and people do join movements for sound reasons, including real injustice. Its value is as a set of questions to ask when a cause demands total commitment. As a description of everyone who has ever held a strong belief, it goes too far.

books.title: Games People Play
books.author: Eric Berne
books.why: Gives you a simple vocabulary for the repeating patterns that trip up everyday relationships.

cards.title: We hunger for recognition
cards.body: Berne starts from the idea that people need to be noticed by others as surely as they need food. He calls a unit of recognition a stroke: a greeting, a smile, a compliment, and also a frown or a criticism. His striking claim is that a negative stroke is better than none, which helps explain why a neglected child misbehaves, and why some adults would sooner quarrel than be ignored.
cards.try: Give three people a real moment of attention today: a proper greeting, a thank-you, or a question about them.

cards.title: Three voices in each of us
cards.body: Berne describes three states we move between. The Parent is the voice of rules and care we absorbed from those who raised us. The Adult weighs facts and deals with the present. The Child holds our early feelings: playfulness, fear, defiance. None is bad, and a healthy person uses all three. The trouble comes when the wrong one answers, as when a simple question is met with a scolding.

cards.title: Crossed wires
cards.body: An exchange goes smoothly when the reply comes from the state that was addressed. "Have you seen my keys?" asks one Adult of another, and "On the table" answers in kind. If the reply is "Why can you never look after your things?", a Parent has answered and addressed a Child, and the exchange is crossed. Talk about the keys stops and a different conversation begins. Noticing the cross is the first step to uncrossing it.
cards.try: The next time a conversation suddenly turns sour, ask yourself which voice just spoke: Parent, Adult or Child.

cards.title: What a game is
cards.body: In Berne's sense, a game is a repeated series of exchanges that looks reasonable on the surface but has a hidden motive and ends in a predictable bad feeling. In one, a person asks for advice and rejects every suggestion with "yes, but". The hidden aim is not to solve the problem but to show that nobody can. Both players leave frustrated, and both will probably play again.

cards.title: Why we keep playing
cards.body: Games persist, Berne argues, because they pay. They fill time, supply strokes, confirm what a person already believes about themselves and others, and keep real closeness at a safe distance. He describes a spouse who complains that their partner holds them back, when the restriction in fact shields them from something they fear to try. The complaint is real, and so is the hidden convenience.

cards.title: Beyond games
cards.body: The alternative Berne offers is autonomy, which he describes through three capacities: awareness of what is happening now, spontaneity in choosing how to respond, and intimacy, meaning honest closeness with no hidden agenda. His scheme is a clinician's framework, not something proven by experiment, and some of its 1960s examples have dated. But as a way of seeing one's own patterns it is still useful.

books.title: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
books.author: Erving Goffman
books.why: A sociologist's classic showing how much of ordinary social life is a careful, shared performance.

cards.title: We are all performing
cards.body: Goffman looks at everyday life through the language of theatre. Whenever we are with others, he argues, we try to guide the impression they form of us, through dress, manner, speech and setting. This is not vanity or deceit. People need to know who they are dealing with in order to act, so each of us offers a version of ourselves suited to the occasion: the patient doctor, the capable applicant.

cards.title: Front stage and back stage
cards.body: In the front region we are before an audience and keep up the standards of the role. In the back region we relax, prepare, and drop the act. Goffman's example is the waiter who is all courtesy in the dining room and quite different through the kitchen door. Everyone needs a backstage. Trouble arises when the audience wanders into it, which is one reason working from home or living with in-laws can be tiring.
cards.try: Notice where your own backstage is, the place you can stop performing, and whether you get enough time there.

cards.title: What we say and what we leak
cards.body: Goffman separates the impressions we give deliberately, mostly in words, from those we give off without meaning to: tone, posture, a glance at the clock. Audiences know the second kind is harder to fake, so they use it to check the first. A host says "do stay", and the guest reads the truth from how it was said. Much social skill lies in reading, and managing, this second channel.

cards.title: Performances are team efforts
cards.body: We rarely perform alone. A family receiving guests, staff in front of customers, a couple at a party: each is a team cooperating to sustain one impression. Members rely on each other not to give the game away, and disagreements are kept for later. This explains the particular sting when a partner contradicts you in front of others. The disagreement matters less than the broken teamwork.

cards.title: Audiences help the show along
cards.body: Onlookers usually cooperate with a performance. We pretend not to hear a stomach rumble, look away from a slip, and accept a thin excuse so that nobody is embarrassed. Goffman calls this tact. Social life depends on the constant small mercy of people helping each other save face. A person who refuses to play along, pointing out every stumble, is soon avoided.
cards.try: The next time someone makes a small blunder in front of you, help them pass over it smoothly.

cards.title: The mask and the face
cards.body: It would be easy to conclude that everyone is a fraud. Goffman's view is subtler. A performer may believe completely in the part, and roles played long enough become second nature: the new parent or manager who starts by acting the role ends by being it. He is less concerned with the question of a true self behind the masks than with how, between us, we keep everyday life running.

books.title: How Emotions Are Made
books.author: Lisa Feldman Barrett
books.why: A leading researcher's challenge to the idea that emotions are fixed reactions wired into us.

cards.title: No fingerprints for feelings
cards.body: The traditional view says each emotion, such as anger, fear or joy, has its own built-in circuit, facial expression and bodily signature. Barrett reviews the evidence and argues that no such consistent fingerprints have been found. A person can be angry with a pounding heart or a steady one, scowling or smiling. Variation, she says, is the rule. Her theory is influential but still debated by researchers who hold the older view.

cards.title: The brain predicts, then checks
cards.body: Barrett's alternative begins with the idea that the brain does not wait passively for the world to act on it. It constantly guesses what is about to happen, based on past experience, and corrects the guess against what arrives. In her account an emotion is one such construction: the brain's best explanation, using concepts it has learned, of what the sensations in your body mean in this situation.

cards.title: Your body budget
cards.body: The brain's main job, Barrett says, is to manage the body's resources: energy, water, salt, rest. She calls this the body budget. When the account runs low through poor sleep, hunger or illness, we feel unpleasant without knowing why, and the brain may explain that feeling as worry, irritation or gloom about whatever is in front of us. Looking after the body is, on this view, a way of looking after feelings.
cards.try: When you next feel low or irritable, check the basics first: when did you last sleep well, eat, drink water, move?

cards.title: A bad feeling is not always a verdict
cards.body: Barrett distinguishes simple feeling, pleasant or unpleasant, stirred up or calm, from full emotions. The simple feeling is always there in the background and colours how we see things, so we take it as information about the world: this plan is bad, this person is annoying. Sometimes it is only a tired body. Knowing this gives a small but real freedom to question a mood before acting on it.

cards.title: More words, finer control
cards.body: People differ in how precisely they tell their feelings apart. Some have only "good" and "bad"; others separate being disappointed from being discouraged, resentful or ashamed.
