Barrett calls this emotional granularity and argues that finer distinctions give the brain better options for what to do next. Learning new words for feelings, in any language, is a practical way to build it.
cards.try: The next time you would say you feel "bad" or "stressed", look for a more exact word for what it is.

cards.title: Emotions are learned with a culture
cards.body: If emotions are built from concepts, they must be learned, and Barrett argues that children pick up the emotion concepts of their culture much as they pick up its language. Different cultures divide feeling in different ways, and some have emotions that others lack a word for. This does not make emotions unreal, any more than money is unreal. It makes them something we take part in making.

books.title: Descartes' Error
books.author: Antonio Damasio
books.why: A neurologist's case that feeling is not the enemy of good reasoning but a necessary part of it.

cards.title: The man who was no longer himself
cards.body: Damasio opens with Phineas Gage, a railway foreman in the 1840s who survived an iron rod passing through the front of his brain. By the accounts that have come down to us he could still walk, speak and remember, but the dependable man was gone, replaced by someone unreliable and unable to stick to plans. The historical record is thin and some details are disputed, but the case first tied the frontal brain to character and judgement.

cards.title: Intelligent, and unable to decide
cards.body: The book's key modern case is a patient Damasio calls Elliot, who had surgery for a tumour at the front of his brain. His memory, language and test scores remained excellent. Yet he could no longer hold a job or manage his affairs, and could spend hours weighing a trivial choice. He was also strangely unmoved by his own misfortunes. Damasio came to think the two changes were one.

cards.title: Gut feelings mark the options
cards.body: Damasio's proposal is that past experience leaves bodily feelings attached to kinds of outcomes. When we consider an option, a faint echo of that feeling, good or bad, arrives before conscious reasoning does, steering us away from some choices and toward others. Without it every option looks equally plausible and deciding never ends. The idea is influential, though the experiments used to test it remain disputed.
cards.try: When stuck between two options, imagine having chosen each in turn and notice what your body does.

cards.title: Reason needs emotion
cards.body: We tend to think the best decisions are made coldly. Damasio accepts that strong emotion can wreck judgement, but argues that too little is just as damaging. Feelings tell us what matters, and without them reasoning has nothing to aim at. A person choosing a job by spreadsheet alone, ignoring a steady sense of dread about one option, is leaving out evidence, not being rigorous.

cards.title: The error
cards.body: The title refers to the old idea, linked to Descartes, that the mind is a separate thing from the body and that pure thought runs free of flesh. Damasio argues the reverse. Mind arises from a brain that is in constant exchange with the body, and the state of the body shapes thought at every step. On this view, sleep, illness and physical ease are part of how well we think, not distractions from it.

books.title: The Seven Sins of Memory
books.author: Daniel L. Schacter
books.why: A memory researcher's tidy map of the ways memory fails, and why those failures are a fair price.

cards.title: Fading, and never storing at all
cards.body: Schacter names seven ways memory goes wrong. The first is transience: memories weaken with time, fastest soon after the event. The second, absent-mindedness, is different. The keys were never lost from memory, because where you put them was never recorded; your attention was elsewhere. This is why going over where you might have left something works less well than paying attention when you set it down.
cards.try: Today, each time you put down your keys or phone, say out loud where you are putting them.

cards.title: On the tip of the tongue
cards.body: The third sin is blocking: the information is stored, you know that you know it, and it will not come. Names of people are the usual victims, because a name has no natural link to anything else about the person. Blocking grows more common with age and is normal. Straining often makes it worse, as a wrong name keeps getting in the way. Leave it, and the right one tends to arrive later unasked.

cards.title: Right memory, wrong source
cards.body: Misattribution is recalling something correctly while being wrong about where it came from: you think you read it in a newspaper when a friend told you, or you take an idea you once heard to be your own. Suggestibility goes further. Leading questions and other people's accounts can add details, or whole events, to a memory. Schacter shows why this matters so much for the testimony of eyewitnesses.

cards.title: The present rewrites the past
cards.body: Schacter calls the sixth sin bias. What we know and feel now shapes how we remember then. We recall our earlier opinions as closer to today's than they were, believe we saw an outcome coming once we know it, and remember ourselves as a little better than we were. Couples who are unhappy now tend to recall their early days as worse than they described them at the time.
cards.try: Before a decision plays out, write down what you expect to happen. Later, compare the note with what you remember thinking.

cards.title: Memories that will not leave
cards.body: The seventh sin is the reverse of forgetting: persistence, the unwanted return of memories we would prefer to lose, such as a humiliation, a failure, or a frightening event. Schacter explains that emotionally charged experiences are stored especially strongly, which is usually useful. When such memories are frequent and distressing, as can happen after trauma, it is something to take to a professional.

cards.title: Flaws that come with the design
cards.body: Schacter's conclusion is reassuring. Each sin is the cost of a feature that serves us well. Forgetting clears away what is no longer needed. A memory that keeps the gist and drops detail lets us generalise. A system that builds memories afresh each time can also imagine the future. A memory that kept everything exactly would be a burden, so occasional failure is the price of one that works.

books.title: Moonwalking with Einstein
books.author: Joshua Foer
books.why: A journalist's year among memory champions, and what their methods reveal about how memory works.

cards.title: Trained, not gifted
cards.body: Foer went to report on a memory championship, expecting to meet people born with unusual brains. The competitors insisted their memories were average and that anyone could learn their methods. He took up the challenge, trained for a year with a coach, and won the United States contest himself. The lesson is that remembering is largely a matter of technique and attention, not a fixed gift.

cards.title: The memory palace
cards.body: The central technique is ancient. Our memory for places and routes is far stronger than our memory for words or numbers, so you turn what you need to remember into images and set them, one by one, along a route through a building you know well. To recall, you walk the route in your mind and see what is there. A shopping list becomes a series of strange scenes in your childhood home.
cards.try: Place five items from your shopping list as odd images in five spots along the way from your front door to your kitchen.

cards.title: Make it strange
cards.body: The mind lets ordinary things slip and keeps what is odd, funny, rude or moving. So the images have to be vivid. Foer also describes a puzzle: told that a man is a baker, people remember it better than if told his name is Baker. The job calls up smells, a white hat and bread, while the name connects to nothing. To remember something, give it hooks into what you already know.
cards.try: When you meet someone new today, tie their name to a vivid picture connected with how they look.

cards.title: Knowledge is what memory hangs on
cards.body: Foer reports research on chess masters, who can recall a board position at a glance, but only when the pieces are arranged as in a real game. They are not remembering thirty-two separate pieces; they recognise a few familiar patterns. Expertise works like this in every field. The more you know about a subject, the easier it is to learn more of it, since each new fact has somewhere to attach.

cards.title: Getting past the plateau
cards.body: In any skill we improve quickly, reach a level that is good enough, and then stop improving while we run on autopilot. Foer learned from researchers on expertise that the way through is to stay out of autopilot on purpose: work at the edge of your ability, watch closely for mistakes, and study them. It is uncomfortable, which is why most of us type, drive or cook no better than we did years ago.

cards.title: What the tricks cannot do
cards.body: Foer is candid about the limits. After his win he still mislaid things and forgot errands like anyone else. The techniques suit lists, numbers and names, and take effort to apply. What stayed with him was a larger point: to remember, you must first pay attention. He suggests that a life filled with noticed, distinct experiences also feels longer and fuller when you look back on it.

books.title: Blink
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.why: An engaging look at snap judgements: when to trust them, and when they lead us badly astray.

cards.title: Thin slices
cards.body: Gladwell's subject is the judgement made in the first seconds of meeting a person or a problem. He calls the ability to find a pattern in a very small sample of experience thin-slicing. He opens with art experts who felt at a glance that a costly ancient statue was wrong, before they could say why, while lengthy tests had passed it. In a field you know deeply, a first impression can hold years of learning.

cards.title: The locked door
cards.body: We often cannot explain where a quick judgement came from. The work happens out of sight, and when asked for reasons we tend to supply plausible ones that may not be the real ones. Gladwell warns that forcing an explanation can even spoil a good instinct. This cuts both ways: it is a reason to respect an expert's unexplained unease, and a reason to doubt our confident stories about why we chose.

cards.title: Signals in a short conversation
cards.body: Gladwell describes a researcher who watches couples talk briefly and looks for particular patterns, treating contempt, such as eye-rolling and sneering, as the most worrying sign. The broader point is that a relationship's habits show up in small samples. The very high prediction rates quoted for this work have been criticised on statistical grounds, so take the idea and leave the percentages.
cards.try: In your next disagreement with someone close, watch for contempt in your own tone or face, and soften it.

cards.title: When first impressions go wrong
cards.body: Snap judgements also carry our prejudices. Gladwell uses the example of a tall, handsome man who looks like a leader and is trusted as one whatever his ability. Quick associations about height, race or sex can steer us without our knowledge or consent. He cites a well-known test of such hidden associations; how well that test measures any individual's bias is disputed among researchers.

cards.title: Change what the eye can see
cards.body: Since we cannot simply will our instant reactions to be fair, Gladwell suggests changing the conditions under which we judge. His main example is orchestras that began auditioning musicians behind a screen, after which more women were hired. Later analysts have questioned how large that effect was, but the principle is sound: where looks are irrelevant, remove them from view.
cards.try: The next time you assess someone's work, try reading it before you know who did it.

cards.title: Less information, less panic
cards.body: Two things spoil rapid judgement. One is too much information: Gladwell tells of a hospital where doctors judged chest pain more accurately using a few key measures than with everything they could gather. The other is extreme stress, which narrows perception until instinct fails. Good snap decisions come from experience and a slowed-down situation, not from simply going with your gut every time.

books.title: The Power Paradox
books.author: Dacher Keltner
books.why: A social psychologist on how influence is really won, and why having it tends to spoil us.

cards.title: Power is in every relationship
cards.body: Keltner defines power as the capacity to make a difference in the world by influencing the states of other people. On that definition it is not limited to bosses and politicians. It is present between parents and children, among friends, in a team, even at a dinner table. Seeing this makes the subject personal: the question is no longer what the powerful are like, but how you handle your own influence.

cards.title: Groups give power, and can take it back
cards.body: The old view holds that power is seized by force and cunning. Keltner argues that in everyday groups it is mostly granted: people give respect and influence to those who advance the good of the group, and withdraw it through gossip and loss of reputation from those who do not. Watch any new team for a few weeks and you can see standing drift toward the people others find helpful.

cards.title: What keeps it
cards.body: In Keltner's account, lasting influence rests on a handful of plain habits: paying real attention to what others feel, giving and sharing, expressing gratitude, and telling stories that bring people together. These are the same behaviours that earned the influence to begin with. They cost little. A thank-you that is specific, or credit given in public, strengthens both the other person and your standing.
cards.try: Thank one person today for something specific they did, and say what difference it made.

cards.title: The paradox
cards.body: Here is the twist. Feeling powerful tends to wear away the very qualities that won the power. Keltner reports studies in which people made to feel powerful become less attentive to others, more impulsive, and readier to think the rules are for someone else. Some of these experiments are small and have been hard to reproduce, so hold the details loosely. The overall pattern matches long experience.
cards.try: In the next conversation where you are the senior person, ask two questions before you give your opinion.

cards.title: What powerlessness does
cards.body: Keltner gives equal weight to the other end. People with little power, through poverty, low rank or discrimination, live with more threat and less control. He reviews evidence linking this to chronic stress, poorer health and narrowed attention. It reframes some behaviour often put down to poor character. Giving people a voice and some real control is, on this view, a matter of health as well as fairness.

books.title: Trauma and Recovery
books.author: Judith Lewis Herman
books.why: A landmark book that showed how survivors of very different horrors share one pattern and one path back.

cards.title: One pattern, many causes
cards.body: Herman's first insight was to place side by side people who had rarely been compared: soldiers back from combat, survivors of rape, of violence at home and of abuse in childhood. She showed that their suffering takes the same basic form. She also observes that society keeps learning about trauma and then forgetting, because the subject is painful, and that it takes public support to keep it in view.

cards.title: Three kinds of aftermath
cards.body: Herman groups the effects into three. Hyperarousal: the body stays on permanent alert, startling easily and sleeping badly. Intrusion: the event breaks back in through flashbacks and nightmares. Constriction: a numbing and shutting down, a narrowing of life to avoid reminders. Survivors can swing between reliving and numbness. Seeing these as known responses to overwhelming events can ease the fear of going mad.

cards.title: Prolonged harm is different
cards.body: A single terrible event is one thing. Herman argues that repeated harm over months or years, where a person is under another's control and cannot leave, as in captivity, abusive homes or childhood abuse, does deeper damage to identity, trust and the capacity for relationships. She proposed a separate diagnosis for this, complex post-traumatic stress disorder, an idea since widely taken up.

cards.title: Recovery belongs to the survivor
cards.body: Trauma, Herman writes, takes away power and cuts a person off from others. So recovery rests on restoring both: the survivor must be in charge of their own recovery, and it can only happen in relationship, not in isolation. Well-meaning helpers who take over repeat the loss of control. The useful stance is to offer support, information and company, and leave the decisions with the person.
cards.try: If someone confides a painful experience, resist giving advice. Ask what would help, and let them decide.

cards.title: Three stages
cards.body: Herman describes recovery as unfolding in three stages. First, establishing safety: of the body, of the living situation, of daily routine. Second, remembrance and mourning: telling the story and grieving what was lost. Third, reconnecting with ordinary life and other people. The stages overlap and people circle back. This is a description, not a self-help plan; the work is best done with a trained professional.

cards.title: The role of the witness
cards.body: Herman points out that bystanders are pulled to take a side. The one who did the harm asks only that we do nothing: look away, doubt, forget. The one who was harmed asks us to share a burden of pain. That is why victims are so often disbelieved. Being a good witness is simple to describe and hard to do: listen, believe, and do not rush the person to get over it.

books.title: The Wisdom of Crowds
books.author: James Surowiecki
books.why: Explains when a group's combined judgement beats its smartest member, and when groups go wrong.

cards.title: The crowd that weighed an ox
cards.body: Surowiecki opens with a story from a country fair a century ago, where visitors paid to guess the weight of an ox. A scientist who gathered the hundreds of guesses expected the average to be poor. It was almost exactly right, and better than nearly every individual. Each guess held some information and some error; when combined, the errors pointed in different directions and largely cancelled.

cards.title: Four conditions
cards.body: A crowd is wise only under certain conditions. Its members need diverse views and information. They need to form their opinions independently, not by copying each other. Knowledge should be decentralised, with people drawing on what they know locally. And there must be some way of combining the separate judgements into one. Take away any of these and a crowd can be more foolish than any of its members.

cards.title: Difference beats brilliance
cards.body: Surowiecki argues that a group of varied people often does better than a group made up only of the most expert, because the experts tend to know the same things and share the same blind spots. Adding someone who thinks differently brings new information even if that person is less skilled. When putting together a team or asking for advice, look for the view you do not yet have.
cards.try: On a question you are weighing, ask someone whose background is quite unlike yours and your usual advisers'.

cards.title: Independence is fragile
cards.body: People watch each other. Once the first few have chosen, those who follow may set aside their private judgement and go along, on the reasonable assumption that the others know something. Soon everyone is following everyone and nobody's knowledge is being used. Surowiecki uses this to explain fashions, market bubbles and crashes. A crowded restaurant shows that people are there, not that the food is good.

cards.title: Coordination and cooperation
cards.body: Not all group problems are about finding a right answer. Some are about coordinating, as when pedestrians pass smoothly on a busy pavement with no one in charge. Others are about cooperating when each person is tempted to let the rest do the work, as with paying taxes or keeping a shared kitchen clean. Surowiecki shows that groups often solve these through conventions and trust more than through orders.

cards.title: Why small groups disappoint
cards.body: Committees and teams often fall short of what their members know. Talk tends to be led by whoever is most senior or speaks most, people give more weight to what everyone has already heard, and discussion can push a like-minded group toward a more extreme view. Surowiecki's fixes are simple: gather opinions before the talk begins, and make sure dissent is voiced.
cards.try: At your next meeting, collect each person's view in writing before anyone speaks.

books.title: Victims of Groupthink
books.author: Irving L. Janis
books.why: The study that gave us the word groupthink, and practical steps for stopping a team from fooling itself.

cards.title: When harmony beats judgement
cards.body: Janis studied how groups of able, well-informed advisers arrived at disastrous decisions, with the failed 1961 landing at the Bay of Pigs in Cuba as his leading case. His answer was groupthink: in a close-knit group the wish to stay agreed can quietly override the job of weighing alternatives realistically. No one is stupid or forced. The members like and respect each other, and that is where the problem lies.

cards.title: The feeling of being right and safe
cards.body: The first signs Janis lists concern how the group sees itself and others. Members share an unspoken sense that such a capable team cannot fail, explain away warnings together, take for granted that their cause is moral, and hold a crude picture of opponents as weak or foolish. When a team stops asking "what if we are wrong?" and starts mocking outsiders, the conditions are in place.

cards.title: Silence mistaken for agreement
cards.body: The other signs concern pressure toward sameness. Anyone who voices doubt is gently reminded to be loyal. Members with reservations keep quiet so as not to spoil the mood. Since nobody objects, everyone concludes that all agree. And some appoint themselves guards, keeping unwelcome facts from the leader. The outcome is a room of private doubters, each assuming they are alone.
cards.try: In your next group decision, ask each person to name one risk before anyone is allowed to say they agree.

cards.title: What makes it likely
cards.body: Janis found groupthink most likely when a group is tightly bonded, cut off from outside opinion, led by someone who states a preference early, and under pressure to decide. His evidence is a set of historical case studies. Later experiments have given mixed support, and closeness alone does not reliably cause it. The clearest risks are an insulated group and a leader who shows their hand first.

cards.title: The same people, a better process
cards.body: Janis contrasts the Bay of Pigs with the Cuban missile crisis the following year, handled by largely the same leader and advisers. The process had changed. The president sometimes stayed out of the room so people would speak freely, the group split into smaller teams that worked separately, outside experts were heard, and objections were invited. The people were the same. The rules of discussion had been improved.

cards.title: Building in the doubt
cards.body: From this Janis drew remedies any team can use. The leader holds back their own view at the start. Someone is given the job of arguing against the favoured plan, and the role rotates so it is taken seriously. Outsiders are asked in to challenge. And once a decision seems settled, a further meeting is held at which everyone is urged to voice any remaining doubts.
cards.try: If you lead a discussion this week, give your own opinion last.

books.title: How We Know What Isn't So
books.author: Thomas Gilovich
books.why: A clear guide to how sensible people come to hold mistaken beliefs, and how to check your own.

cards.title: Seeing streaks in chance
cards.body: We expect random events to look evenly mixed, so when chance produces a run we assume something is behind it. Gilovich's well-known example is the belief that basketball players get a "hot hand"; his analysis of shooting records found no more streaks than chance would give. Later researchers have argued a modest hot hand may exist after all. Either way, we see far more pattern in randomness than is there.

cards.title: Extremes drift back to average
cards.body: An unusually good or bad result is partly luck, so the next is likely to be more ordinary. We overlook this and credit whatever we did in between. Gilovich notes a cruel effect: we tend to praise after a great performance and scold after a poor one, then watch the first decline and the second improve, and conclude that scolding works and praise does not. Neither may have had any effect.
cards.try: The next time something improves right after you intervened, ask whether it would have improved anyway.

cards.title: The evidence we never see
cards.body: Many beliefs rest on only part of the picture. An interviewer is sure of their eye for talent, but sees only how the people they hired turned out, never how the rejected ones would have done. A remedy seems to work because we rarely try doing nothing. Gilovich's point is that we judge by the cases in front of us and forget to ask about the cases that our own choices kept out of sight.

cards.title: Two standards of proof
cards.body: We do not weigh evidence evenly. For a conclusion we like, Gilovich observes, we ask only whether the evidence permits us to believe it. For one we dislike, we ask whether the evidence forces us to. The first test is easy to pass and the second almost impossible. We end up sincerely feeling that we followed the facts, having in truth set a different bar for each side.
cards.try: Take a belief you are fond of and apply the test you would use on a claim you dislike.

cards.title: Stories improve in the telling
cards.body: Much of what we know comes secondhand, and tellers want to be interesting. With each retelling the awkward details and qualifications drop out and the striking parts are sharpened, until a rumour or news item is tidier and more dramatic than what happened. Gilovich advises asking how close the source was to the event, and being most wary of the stories that are most satisfying.

cards.title: Thinking everyone agrees
cards.body: We tend to overestimate how many people share our opinions and habits. One cause is that we mix mostly with people like ourselves. Another is that adults seldom tell each other they disagree; we nod, change the subject, and keep our doubts private. So our beliefs get less correction than we suppose. A view that nobody has challenged has not necessarily been tested.

books.title: The Marshmallow Test
books.author: Walter Mischel
books.why: The creator of a famous experiment explains what self-control is and how it can be learned.

cards.title: The test
cards.body: In the 1960s Mischel offered young children at a nursery a choice: one treat now, or two if they could wait alone with the treat in front of them until the researcher came back. Some ate it within moments; others held out for many minutes. What interested Mischel was not who succeeded but how. Watching through a window, he saw that the children who waited were doing something different.

cards.title: Waiting is a skill, not a clenched jaw
cards.body: The children who lasted did not stare at the sweet and grit their teeth. They looked away, sang, played with their toes, or pretended the treat was only a picture. When Mischel taught such tricks to other children, they waited much longer. Self-control, he concluded, is less a matter of strong will than of strategies for making the temptation weaker, and strategies can be taught.
cards.try: Put the thing that tempts you most, snack or phone, out of sight and in another room for the next two hours.

cards.title: Hot and cool thinking
cards.body: Mischel describes two ways the mind handles a temptation. The hot way is emotional and immediate: it sees the taste, the pleasure, the now. The cool way is slower and more reflective. The children who waited cooled the treat by thinking about its shape or colour, not its sweetness. You can do the same with a craving by describing it in flat, factual terms, or imagining it as a photograph.

cards.title: Decide in advance
cards.body: When the moment of temptation comes, the hot system is already in charge and it is too late to reason. Mischel recommends setting up a plan ahead of time in the form "if this happens, then I will do that", and rehearsing it until it runs without thought. "If the dessert menu comes, then I will order coffee." The decision is made while you are cool, and carried out when you are not.
cards.try: Write one "if ..., then I will ..." plan for a temptation you expect to meet tomorrow.

cards.title: Step back from yourself
cards.body: Strong feelings ease when we view them from a distance. Mischel describes research in which people who recall a painful event as if watching it happen to someone else, from across the room, are less shaken than those who relive it through their own eyes. The same move helps with the future: picturing in detail the person you will be in ten years makes it easier to do something for them now.

cards.title: What the test does and does not predict
cards.body: Mischel's follow-ups found that children who waited longer tended to do better as teenagers and adults, and the book builds on this. A later, larger study with a more varied group of children found the link much weaker, and largely explained by family background. Waiting also depends on whether a child has reason to trust the promise. Treat the test as a window on strategies, not a forecast of anyone's life.

books.title: Scarcity
books.author: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir
books.why: Shows how having too little of anything, money or time, changes how we think and what we overlook.

cards.title: Having too little takes over the mind
cards.body: The authors argue that scarcity is not only a shortage of something; it is a state of mind. Whether the lack is of money, time, food or company, the unmet need captures attention and keeps pulling thought back to itself. The busy person and the poor person, so different in other ways, are caught in the same mental pattern. Seeing the likeness is the book's first step.

cards.title: The upside: sharp focus
cards.body: Scarcity brings a benefit. When something is running short we use it more carefully and concentrate better. A deadline close at hand produces work that weeks of open time did not, and people on a tight budget know prices exactly. The authors call this the focus dividend. It is real, but it comes bundled with a cost, described in the next card, that we do not choose and often do not notice.

cards.title: Tunnel vision
cards.body: Focusing hard on the pressing shortage means everything outside it drops from view. The authors call this tunnelling. While racing to finish a report you skip exercise and forget a birthday; while scrambling to pay this month's rent you let the insurance lapse. These are not judgements that the neglected thing is unimportant. Inside the tunnel it never comes up for consideration at all.
cards.try: Name one important, non-urgent thing your current rush has pushed out of view, and give it ten minutes today.

cards.title: A tax on the mind
cards.body: Because scarcity keeps occupying thought, the authors argue it leaves less mental capacity for everything else: reasoning, planning, self-control. They report studies in which people did worse on thinking tasks while money worries were on their minds. Some laboratory findings in this area have had mixed results when repeated. The central point is a humane one: struggling people may be overloaded, not incapable.

cards.title: Borrowing from tomorrow
cards.body: Inside the tunnel the urgent need is everything and its later cost is faint, so we borrow: money at high interest, or time, by pushing a task to next week, when it will be no easier. Each loan makes the next period tighter still. The authors show how this creates a trap in which people are always one step behind, juggling. Being short of time and being short of money work the same way.

cards.title: Leave some slack
cards.body: The remedy the authors stress is slack: spare room that is not allotted to anything. They describe a hospital whose operating rooms were always fully booked, so every emergency disrupted the schedule; keeping one room free for emergencies let it treat more patients, not fewer. A diary with no gaps or a budget with no buffer will break at the first surprise. Leaving room for surprises is part of planning well.
cards.try: Block one hour this week with nothing in it, and guard it as you would an appointment.

books.title: Strangers to Ourselves
books.author: Timothy D. Wilson
books.why: A psychologist's sober account of how little direct access we have to our own minds, and what to do about it.

cards.title: The mind's hidden workforce
cards.body: Wilson describes an adaptive unconscious: a large set of mental processes that size up situations, set goals, form impressions and start actions without our awareness. Unlike Freud's unconscious it is not a cellar of repressed wishes. It is simply efficient, built for speed, and cannot be inspected. Some studies from this period have failed to replicate, but the central claim that much thinking happens out of view is well supported.

cards.title: We cannot look inside and see why
cards.body: When we explain why we did something, it feels as if we are reporting what we observed in our own minds. Wilson argues that we are usually guessing, using the same common-sense theories an onlooker would use. Experiments show people confidently naming causes that did not affect them and overlooking ones that did. Your account of your own motives is a sensible hypothesis, not a direct reading.

cards.title: Listing reasons can mislead
cards.body: It seems wise to analyse why we feel as we do before choosing. Wilson's research suggests a risk. When asked to list reasons, people fix on what is easy to put into words, shift their view to match, and can end up with a choice they later like less than those who simply chose. For matters of taste, such as a picture for the wall, an informed gut feeling may be the better guide.

cards.title: Watch what you do, and ask others
cards.body: If introspection is limited, Wilson suggests two better sources. One is your own behaviour, observed as an outsider would observe it: what do you really spend time on, return to, avoid? The other is people who know you, who sometimes predict your actions better than you do. Neither is flattering or comfortable, and both can show you what looking inward cannot.
cards.try: Ask someone who knows you well what they think you most enjoy doing, and compare it with your own answer.

cards.title: Act first, and the self follows
cards.body: Since we partly learn who we are by watching what we do, Wilson's advice for change is to begin with the behaviour. Someone who wants to be more considerate should start doing considerate things regularly, without waiting to feel like a considerate person. The actions become habit, and they also become evidence, to yourself, of who you are. The inner change comes after the outer one.
cards.try: Choose one quality you want more of and do one small act today that a person with that quality would do.

books.title: The Unresponsive Bystander
books.author: Bibb Latane and John M. Darley
books.why: The classic experiments on why people in groups fail to help, and how to make sure someone does.

cards.title: The case that started it
cards.body: The authors began their research after the 1964 murder of a young woman in New York, which a newspaper reported as watched by dozens of neighbours who did nothing. That account was later shown to be badly exaggerated. But the question it raised was a good one, and the experiments the authors ran to answer it have held up far better than the original story.

cards.title: More witnesses, less help
cards.body: The central finding is that a person who is the only witness to an emergency is more likely to help, and quicker, than someone who believes others are also present. In one experiment people heard what sounded like a stranger having a seizure over an intercom; those who thought they alone could hear it nearly all went for help, and those who thought several others were listening often did not.

cards.title: Responsibility gets divided
cards.body: One reason is that responsibility spreads out. Alone, the whole duty to act falls on you, and so would the whole blame. Among ten onlookers, each feels only a share of it and assumes that someone else has surely already called for help. Everyone reasons the same way, and nobody calls. The same thing happens when a group email asks "can somebody deal with this?"
cards.try: The next time a message asks a whole group for help, answer it yourself or name the person who will.

cards.title: Everyone looks calm, so it must be fine
cards.body: A second reason is that emergencies are often unclear. Is that man ill or asleep? To decide, we glance at others, who are glancing at us, and each is trying to look composed. Everyone reads the others' calm as a sign that nothing is wrong. In one experiment people sat on in a room filling with smoke because the others present showed no concern.

cards.title: Five steps to helping
cards.body: The authors lay out what has to happen before anyone helps. You must notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, accept that it is your responsibility, know what to do, and then decide to do it. A failure at any step means no help is given. This makes the bystander's inaction understandable as hesitation and confusion at particular points, not as coldness or bad character.

cards.title: Using it
cards.body: If you need help in a crowd, pick out one person and give a clear instruction: "You in the blue jacket, please call an ambulance." That removes the doubt and the shared responsibility at once. If you are the bystander, assume nobody else has acted. Later research offers some comfort: the effect is weaker when the danger is obvious, and in real public incidents someone often does step in.
cards.try: Decide now that if you ever see someone who may need help, you will be the one who checks.
